# Nxeon hypervisor + VM-config performance research

Date: 2026-10-02. Scope: Proxmox host layer and VM config on all 5 nodes. Strictly read-only; nothing was changed on any node. Evidence was taken live at about 17:46-17:50 UTC (a single snapshot, not a time series; "peak hours" behaviour is NOT measured, see section 6).

Node names used below: N1 = primary 51.79.162.96 (SGP, ns5002569), N2 = 178.63.94.114 (FSN, nxeon-fsn1), N3 = 15.235.145.177 (SGP, nxeon-sgp2), N4 = 139.99.125.21 (SGP, ns564103), N5 = 54.39.132.159 (BHS, nxeon-bhs1).

---

## 1. Summary table (prioritised)

| # | Change | Evidence (live) | Benefit | Risk | Needs VM reboot? | New provisions only? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0-1 | Stop host swapping / OOM: fix RAM overcommit on N1, N4 (and N2); `vm.swappiness` 60 to 10; re-balance VMs to N5/N3 | N1 swap 10.2/10.2 GB FULL, N4 swap 2047/2047 MB full with 2 GB free; **host OOM killed VM 8000 (nxeon-mail) on 2026-09-25 12:02** | Removes the biggest latency source: qemu pages sitting in swap = multi-ms stalls for customers | Low for swappiness; medium for moving VMs | N
| P0-2 | Remove the legacy balloon floors on 42 running customer VMs (set `balloon` = `memory`) | 30 of 56 running VMs still have balloon < RAM; ~73 GB total reclaimable; e.g. N2 vm 141 (16 GB plan) balloon 15.4 GB live (actual), N3 vms 107/119/122/125/126 | Customers get the RAM they paid for (was incident on 2026-10-01); but see P0-1: must be done only after capacity is made | Raises real RAM de
| P0-3 | Raise ZFS ARC cap on N2 from 400 MB to 4-8 GB | N2 `zfs_arc_max=409993216`, ARC 385 MB, 13.5 GB RAM free, 100 GB of zvols; ARC hit 87% vs 91% elsewhere | Much better read caching for 12 VMs; the 67.7 s full clone measured 2026-10-01 is a symptom | Low (live, `echo > /sys/module/zfs/parameters/zfs_arc_max`) | No | No |
| P1-1 | Disk: add `iothread=1` (+ `ssd=1`) on scsi0 of every VM and in the clone template config | No VM has `iothread`; `scsihw=virtio-scsi-single` is set but without iothread has little effect | Lower guest-IO latency, less contention in the main qemu thread; most visible on game saves, DB, `apt` | Low; pending until cold restart | Yes (cold stop/start) | New VMs: yes, via template/provision |
| P1-2 | Enable `compression=lz4` on the `data` pool of N1, N3, N4, N5 (N2 already compresses) | `compression=off` on 4 of 5 NVMe pools; host CPUs are mostly idle | Less IO, less NVMe wear (see P1-4), often faster reads on game/OS data. Only applies to newly written blocks | Low | No | Existing VMs benefit only as blocks are rewritten |
| P1-3 | Virtio multiqueue: `net0 ...,queues=<vCPUs>` on VMs (cap at 4) | No VM sets `queues`; all NAT through vmbr1 | Spreads packet processing across vCPUs for busy game/web VMs; small win for 1-2 vCPU plans | Low | Yes | New VMs: yes |
| P1-4 | Plan NVMe replacement: N5 nvme1 at **80 % used (271 TB written)**, N2 pair at 54 %/68 % | SMART "Percentage Used" | Prevents a surprise mirror degradation (and an IO slowdown during resilver) | n/a (hardware) | n/a | n/a |
| P1-5 | Stop running CPU-heavy dev/test jobs on N1 | N1 CPU PSI some avg10 66 %, 33 vCPUs on 8 threads (4.1:1), niced `node` tsx test jobs at nice 19 | Removes CPU scheduling delay for customer VMs on N1 | None | No | n/a |
| P2-1 | `zpool set autotrim=on` (or monthly `zpool trim`) on NVMe pools | `autotrim=off` everywhere, guests use `discard=on` | Steady-state NVMe write performance, no write-cliff | Low-medium (extra IO while trimming) | No | No |
| P2-2 | Move N1 swap off the VM pool / shrink it, or add a plain NVMe swap partition (not a zvol) | N1 swap = 8 GB zvol (sync=always, 4K) on the same mirror as VM disks + 2x1 GB partitions, all full | Avoids swap-to-zvol deadlock risk under memory pressure | Medium (swap changes under pressure) | No | No |
| P2-3 | Network sysctl: BBR + `fq`, `netdev_max_backlog` 5000, `rmem_max/wmem_max` 16 MB | cubic + fq_codel, backlog 1000, 4 MB | TCP throughput on long SGP/EU paths; UDP games unaffected | Low | No | No |
| P2-4 | Ring buffers: raise RX/TX on igb/e1000e hosts (RX 256 to 1024 or more) | N1/N2/N4 RX=256 (max 4096) | Fewer drops under bursts. NIC counters show 0 drops now, so benefit unproven | Low (brief link flap) | No | No |
| P3 | Hugepages for VMs, NUMA, CPU pinning, `mitigations=off` | See section 7 | Small or unsafe on this hardware | `mitigations=off` is a security risk for multi-tenant | n/a | n/a |

Short answer to "what makes everything faster": it is mostly NOT exotic tuning. Customer VMs are already `cpu: host`, virtio net and virtio-scsi, NVMe mirrors, performance governor. The measurable problems are memory pressure (N1, N4), a mis-capped ARC (N2), leftover balloon floors, and CPU contention on N1.

#cloud-config
# Nxeon GOLDEN game template build (scripts/golden/build-golden-template.sh).
# Runs ONCE inside a throwaway clone of the stock Ubuntu 24.04 template (9000),
# pre-installs everything every game provision otherwise downloads on first
# boot, pre-pulls the hottest game images, scrubs per-instance identity, and
# powers off so the caller can convert it into a template.
# Placeholders replaced by the build script: __IMAGES__
package_update: true
packages:
  - qemu-guest-agent
  - unzip
  - git
  - curl
  - ca-certificates
write_files:
  - path: /root/golden-build.sh
    permissions: "0700"
    content: |
      #!/bin/bash
      set -euxo pipefail
      exec > /var/log/nxeon-golden-build.log 2>&1
      systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent || true
      curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh
      systemctl enable docker containerd
      for img in __IMAGES__; do docker pull "$img"; done
      docker image ls --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} {{.Size}}' > /etc/nxeon-golden-images.txt
      echo "built $(date -u +%FT%TZ) from 9000" > /etc/nxeon-golden
      cloud-init status --wait || true
      # Scrub everything per-instance so each clone is a brand-new machine.
      apt-get clean
      rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/partial/* /tmp/* /var/tmp/*
      passwd -d root || true
      passwd -l root || true
      rm -f /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /root/.bash_history
      rm -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*
      truncate -s 0 /etc/machine-id
      rm -f /var/lib/dbus/machine-id
      cloud-init clean --logs --seed
      sync
      fstrim -av || true
      echo GOLDEN_BUILD_OK > /dev/console || true
      poweroff
runcmd:
  - [ bash, -c, "nohup /root/golden-build.sh >/dev/null 2>&1 &" ]

Checking disk requirements across games, most need 10GB or more except bedrock (5GB), cs16/necesse (8GB), so a 12GB virtual disk size would cover nearly everything except those smaller edge cases.

Now I'm compiling per-node capacity stats: thread counts, RAM, running VM counts, vCPU-to-thread ratios, committed RAM percentages, available host RAM/swap, and how many guest VMs fall below their paid RAM allocation on each node (N1 through N4, with N5 still pending).

N5 fills in with low pressure numbers, and I'm noting balloon memory examples consistent with earlier findings about running VMs having balloon actual below paid RAM. I'm now drafting placement policy proposals: refusing or penalizing hosts with low available memory, active swap use, high CPU pressure, or excessive vCPU-to-thread ratios, and adding CPU weighting to the scheduler.

I'm also flagging that capacity numbers in the database look stale compared to actual node RAM, proposing an enforcement mode for the RAM guard, and working out an overcommit policy that caps pinned RAM allocation per node with a safety reserve. Running the numbers, nodes 1-4 are collectively over that cap by roughly 65 GB versus node 5's headroom, suggesting at least one new 64 GB node is needed immediately to relieve the squeeze, though I'm second-guessing whether the "excess" calculation correctly accounts for which RAM is actually pinned versus just allocated.

Actual usage is only about 53% of paid capacity, so there's no imminent OOM everywhere, but node-4 is critically low on available RAM with swap fully used, and node-1 already had a kill event. For the new node spec, I'm recommending matching the existing CPU class but bumping to 128 GB RAM since these nodes are RAM-bound rather than CPU-bound, with mirrored NVMe storage sized to avoid the disk overcommit issues seen on node-4, ECC memory, a spare per region, and 10 GbE networking where supported since most nodes are still on 1G links despite heavy VM density.

I'm also noting that shared 1 Gbps NICs become a bottleneck during simultaneous game downloads or concurrent VM provisioning, and defining concrete triggers for when to add a node — things like sellable RAM headroom dropping below two weeks of growth, MemAvailable under 10% for an hour, swap over 50%, or ZFS pool utilization crossing the 75-80% performance cliff — then estimating SG's growth rate to project how many days current capacity will last.

I'm weighing whether to allow RAM overcommit: real usage runs around 53% of paid allocation, so with free-page-reporting, ballooning, and KSM/zswap you could maybe push 1.1-1.25x on non-game VPS tiers with measured low idle usage, but game VMs running Java heaps or Steam should keep a hard 100% floor with no overcommit.

Looking closer at the Singapore-vs-rest-of-world capacity claim, I realize it's wrong: FSN (Germany) is actually 120% DB-committed with only 14 GB available despite looking roomy, while only BHS (Canada) has genuine headroom at 25 GB available and 47% committed — meaning roughly 20 GB is actually sellable there. But Singapore customers can't just be rerouted to Canada since the latency hit (220+ ms) violates regional placement policy, so I need honored-region constraints in any fix.

For improving node placement scoring within a region, I'm thinking the priority order should be: real sellable headroom first, then live PSI/IO pressure, then whether the template exists, then golden image presence, then local image availability.

Now I'm weighing whether a warm pool of pre-provisioned running VMs is worth the RAM cost — keeping a couple of idle 4 GB Minecraft VMs per region eats roughly 15% of a node's capacity, and stopped pools only cost disk but need 35-45 seconds to boot versus 5-10 seconds for a running pool. I conclude that with golden images plus linked clones and preloaded game-file templates, the cold-start path already gets close to warm-pool speed (~60-90s vs ~20-30s), so warm pools are only worth pursuing after the golden-image pipeline is solid — and even then, pre-provisioned VMs need re-keying at claim time (passwords, management keys, SSH host keys, machine-id) to avoid identity collisions.

I'm also thinking about which plans would benefit most — Minecraft orders and plain Ubuntu VPS make up a meaningful share of real orders, making them the best P3 candidates — and I'm looking at where steps in the provisioning pipeline can run in parallel, like overlapping inventory checks with cloning, or combining NAT and game-port forwarding into the pre-start sync since ports are already known, to shave a few seconds off the critical path.

By front-loading forwards before boot, I can cut two of three sync cycles, saving around six seconds and eliminating a real failure mode I spotted — several provisioning jobs failed because NAT sync errors on one node blocked game port forwarding entirely. I'm also considering pipelining the sequential SSH steps for guest readiness into a single script, running readiness checks and email notifications in parallel with join sync, and tightening polling intervals (SSH and game-port checks) to shave a few more seconds off total provisioning time.

Beyond that, the bigger time sinks are elsewhere: the package update on first boot takes 72 seconds, Docker tooling installation adds another 25+, and Docker Hub image pulls can be huge and throttled, especially when nodes share IPs behind NAT. Steam content downloads are the real elephant though — some games require tens of gigabytes fresh on every server, Minecraft's jar-plus-worldgen takes 30+ seconds, and background installs like the Claude CLI and telemetry shipper compete for resources right when the game is trying to start. Failed provisioning attempts are also costly since they burn through the port window and extended retry period, though at least retries are now idempotent.

Looking at real failure data across 63 jobs since August 4th, I see 51 completed successfully and 12 failed, with a 75% first-attempt success rate overall (much higher for VPS at 95% versus games at 66%). Breaking down the actual failures: four were a Prisma unique constraint bug now fixed, two were Valheim duplicate IP issues, two were PZ blank admin username bugs, one was CS2's sellability blocker, one was a Node.js parameter verification bug, and two were unexplained Minecraft game-port timeouts.

So essentially all failures trace back to bugs that are now fixed or known unsellable configs — but the 66% first-try rate for games is still concerning, and the sweep data from October 1st shows the "game port never opened" pattern dominates for larger or Steam-based families, which points to the 300-second window and install time as the real bottleneck.

I think I have enough to compose a roadmap now. My top priority for this week is baking the agent, unzip, curl, git, and ca-certificates directly into the stock Ubuntu template per node, which should save 70-100 seconds on every provision by skipping redundant package installs. I'm sketching out the implementation — reusing the existing golden template build script, loosening the clone-source gate to allow non-game Ubuntu 24.04 orders, and planning a low-risk canary rollout on node-5 and node-4 with five test provisions each to measure the actual time savings via new per-phase timestamps.

For Docker, I'm deciding it should only go into a separate "game-base" template rather than the general VPS template, since running a Docker daemon by default on plain VPS instances could be surprising and adds unnecessary overhead — so I'll split into "base" (just the agent tooling) and "game-base" (agent plus Docker) templates. Beyond that, I'm noting the ARC clone-speed fix as another quick win, phase-timing instrumentation as a small but necessary P0 to properly measure everything, and NAT sync consolidation as a lower-priority P2 item. For P1, I'm thinking about building per-family golden image tiers for top games like Minecraft, Valheim, Terraria, and Rust, distributed via send/receive from a build node, along with a registry mirror to speed up repeated pulls.

Now I'm weighing whether to build per-family Steam templates versus a shared lancache approach: given the low order volume per family per node (only ~13 of 44 game orders over 60 days spread across 5 nodes and 12 Steam families), repeat-hit rates for a cache would be too rare to justify the ROI, making dedicated golden templates for high-volume families like Valheim and Rust the more effective choice despite the long install times they're meant to offset.

I'm sizing the disk footprint: roughly 48 GB total across Valheim, PZ, Rust, Palworld, and ARK templates per node, which fits comfortably on pools with ample free space (N5, N3, N2) but should be skipped on overcommitted nodes like N4 and N1. For implementation, I'd need to run each game's real setup script once to download the server files, then strip out per-server state like world saves, configs, and passwords before baking the template, since the entrypoint logic (e.g., in the lloesche image) checks for existing install directories and expects clean server files without pre-existing session data.

I need to be careful that template-building doesn't leave stale secrets baked in -- using dummy passwords during the build and verifying the wipe is complete before powering off, with verification scripts to confirm this. Beyond that, there's a second tier of work: standing up warm pools for Minecraft/Ubuntu, template drift detection with a versioned registry, capacity fixes (adding a new node with 128GB+ RAM, enforcing RAM guards, re-pinning balloon floors, fixing capacityRamMB, tuning swappiness), and finally compiling a table of expected gains per metric.

For measurement, I'm thinking about adding phase timestamps to the Job model -- either a new JSON column tracking each provisioning step's timing, or storing a timeline on the Server record, plus recording clone source and golden template flags. This would let me build p50/p90 provisioning reports per node/family/template as an SLO.

For canary rollout, I like that the current per-node template detection naturally gives canary behavior -- building the golden template only on one node first means other nodes automatically stay on stock until it's proven out, though I need to resolve the mismatch where different nodes have different vmids for the same template.

Since the env var approach is platform-wide and vmids are never reused on rebuild, I'm realizing the better design is moving the golden template mapping into the database per-node (something like Node.goldenTemplates), which would allow proper per-node rollout and version pinning -- recording which template vmid/version each server was built from so reinstalls stay consistent. I also need to flag data limitations: startedAt timestamps only exist since October 1st, so true run-time is only available for a subset of jobs, with everything before affected by a guest-agent bug adding ~180s, and phase-level timing isn't persisted anywhere yet, just reconstructed from logs.

Looking at the four clean October 2nd provisions, I'm breaking down the timeline into claim-to-start, boot-to-verified, game-stage, and tail segments for each job type -- Minecraft, Ubuntu, Terraria, and Core Keeper -- to see where the 112-148 second boot window and the game-specific setup time actually go, noting that the game stage mostly reflects time until the join port opens.

Beyond the measured docker-pull times, there's still roughly 100 seconds unaccounted for in Terraria and Core Keeper's game stage that I can't fully explain -- possibly apt-get overhead or world generation -- so I'm being upfront that this part is a guess.

I'm also sketching a hypothetical "golden image" path with preloaded containers and warm boots to estimate potential savings: roughly 60% faster across Minecraft, VPS, and Valheim scenarios, though I'm flagging these as medium-confidence estimates since only a couple of data points (guest-agent and docker startup times) were actually measured. Now I'm ready to write this up, keeping the numbers internally consistent and clearly separating verified data from estimates, with an appendix pointing to the raw scripts.

# Nxeon performance research: provisioning pipeline, templates, capacity and placement

Date: 2026-10-02. Strictly read-only (repo, SELECT-only DB scripts, read-only SSH/pvesh on the 5 nodes, `journalctl` on the worker, public Docker registry metadata). Nothing was changed, restarted, provisioned or loaded. Scripts used are in `/root/research/scripts/` (q1..q6.ts, an.py, nodeinfo.sh, cap.sh, zfs.sh, tasks.sh).

Node names: N1 = primary (51.79.162.96, SGP), N2 = node-2 (FSN, Hetzner), N3 = node-3 (SGP, "sgp2"), N4 = node-4 (SGP), N5 = node-5 (BHS, Canada).

Companion reports (written in parallel, not repeated here): `perf-hypervisor.md` (host tuning), `perf-guest-and-games.md` (in-guest and per-game tuning). Where they overlap I cite them.

---

## 0. Evidence quality, read this first

- **There is no per-phase timing stored anywhere.** `Job` keeps createdAt/startedAt/finishedAt and only the *last* step label (`Job.step`, `Server.provisioningStep`). `startedAt` only exists for jobs since 2026-10-01 (54 of 185 PROVISION rows). So "time per phase" below is **derived** from three independent sources: (a) worker journald markers (claim, snippet write, the three NAT-sync bursts, DONE), (b) Proxmox task logs on the nodes (clone/config/start durations), (c) in-guest numbers already measured in `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` and `perf-guest-and-games.md`. Phases inside the guest (cloud-init package step, docker install, pull, game init) are **not separable from the DB**; they are inferred. Roadmap item R0 fixes this.
- Durations before 2026-10-01 contain the old guest-agent bug (a fixed 180 s wait on every provision, fixed 10-01). I use post-fix runs (10-02) for the baseline and say so.
- 122 of the 185 PROVISION rows have no surviving Server row. 81 of those are the 2026-10-01 all-families catalog sweep (test servers on N5, queue-delayed, many deliberately huge or broken games). They are excluded from production-like statistics. 63 jobs have a live Server row ("real").
- Order volume is small (44 new servers in 30 days, 17 in the last 7), so per-family/per-node cells have n of 1 to 15. Medians for n<5 are anecdotes.

---

## 1. Summary table (prioritised roadmap)

Gains are seconds off a *typical* provision unless stated. "Confidence" is how much of the number is measured vs estimated.

| # | Change | Expected gain | Confidence | Effort | Risk | Rollout / canary |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **R0** | Persist per-phase timestamps for every PROVISION (additive `Job.phases` JSON, written from `step()` plus a few extra marks), admin p50/p90 by family/node/template | 0 s itself; makes every other number measurable | n/a | S (half a day) | Very low (additive column) | Ship first, before R1 |
| **R1** | Bake `qemu-guest-agent`, `unzip`, `curl`, `git`, `ca-certificates` into a new Ubuntu 24.04 base template (VPS flavour, no Docker) and clone it for plain-Ubuntu VPS orders. Today only *game* orders can use a pre-baked template (`chooseCloneSource` returns stock for non-game) | **~70-100 s off every Ubuntu VPS** (165 s now to ~60-75 s). Measured: the stock first boot spends 72 s in `package_update` + 2 packages; baked guests answer the agent ~15 s after start | High on the saving (72 s measured twice), medium on the final total | S | Low | Build on N5 first (template presence is the per-node switch), 5 canary orders, then N4/N3/N2. Instant rollback: delete/untag the template |
| **R2** | Turn on the golden path that already exists for games (`NXEON_GOLDEN_GAME_TEMPLATE` + `NXEON_GOLDEN_LINKED_CLONE=1`), **after** rebuilding the template smaller (virtual 9-10 G, not 12 G) and with a better image set, per node, starting with N5 | **~130-170 s off every game provision** (Minecraft 250 to ~100-120, Terraria/Core Keeper 255-285 to ~100-120). Docker install + pull (+25 s measured, more in practice) and the 72 s package step disappear; clone drops 5-25 s to ~2 s | Medium-high. POC measured on N2 on 10-01: guest agent ~15 s, docker +1.2 s, linked clone 2.1 s. End-to-end totals are my estimate | M | Low-medium (template staleness, linked-clone dependency, see 4.6) | **Not enabled in prod today** (env unset, verified on the worker process). Only N2 has the POC template 9101 (12 G, 3 images). Roll N5, then N3/N2/N4 |
| **R3** | Node-local Docker Hub pull-through cache (`registry:2` proxy on each node's vmbr1 gateway) + authenticated Docker Hub pulls + `Node.registryMirror` instead of the global env var; pin images by digest | 10-60 s per first pull of an uncached image; removes the shared-NAT-IP rate-limit/abort failure class (RCA valheim-gjjrv9) | Medium (pull sizes measured: 150-1240 MB compressed; speed not) | M | Low (Docker falls back to upstream if the mirror is dead) | Hook already built (`NXEON_DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR`); needs the cache + per-node column. N2 first (single NAT IP, only Hetzner node) |
| **R4** | Game-file templates for the Steam families that dominate install time (Valheim 2.1 GB, Project Zomboid 6.9 GB, Rust, Palworld, ARK 22.9 GB): linked clone of a VM whose `/opt/<game>` is already installed | Valheim 400 s to ~100-130 s; PZ 372 to ~120; ARK 1269 to ~150-200; Rust 1475 (3 attempts) to ~150 | Medium-low (no clone of a game-file template has been tried; the steam delta on start is unknown) | L | Medium (per-server secrets/worlds must never leak into a template; weekly rebuild; extra disk) | N5 first, behind a per-family flag, families by observed order volume |
| **R5** | Fix N2's ZFS ARC cap (400 MB) per `perf-hypervisor.md` P0-3 | Stock clone on N2 is 13-25 s vs 4-8 s elsewhere; golden full clone 63-67 s. Expected clone ~5-8 s | Medium | S | Low | Live sysfs change on N2 |
| **R6** | NAT-sync consolidation and parallelism: allocate game/join forwards before start, sync once; run IP inventory in parallel with the clone; sync only the target node; one SSH session for access+identity+key; poll SSH every 2 s and TCP game port every 3 s | **~15-25 s** total | Low-medium (each piece is 2-8 s, only the three NAT bursts are directly visible) | M | Low-medium (NAT path is delicate) | Behind a flag, canary N5 |
| **R7** | Capacity: add >=1 Singapore node now (recommended 12+ threads, 128 GB RAM class, mirrored NVMe >=960 GB), enforce the RAM guard, schedule on live PSI/swap/CPU not only DB plan-RAM, stop selling pinned RAM beyond 0.95 x (RAM - 12 GB) | Removes host swap/OOM and the per-VM latency it causes; lets the 17 squeezed VMs be re-pinned to full RAM | High on the problem, medium on the sizing | M (order + onboarding) | Low | See section 5 |
| **R8** | Template drift control: per-node template registry (vmid, version, build date, ZFS guid, image digests) in the DB; read-only drift sweep; `Server.templateVmid` recorded; build once and `zfs send` to nodes | Reliability; prevents "node X has a different/older image" | High that drift exists (section 4.4) | M | Low | Sweep is read-only first |
| **R9** | Warm pool (running pre-provisioned VMs) for Minecraft and plain Ubuntu | A further 20-40 s beyond R1/R2 | Low | L | Medium-high (identity re-keying, RAM held idle) | Only after R1+R2 have been measured. Probably not worth it |

If only three things are done: **R0 + R1 + R2** (about 3-4 days of work, no new infrastructure) and **R7** in parallel because it is a lead-time item.

---

## 2. What provisioning really takes (measured)

### 2.1 Run time by type (DB, jobs with a live server, first-attempt successes, `updatedAt - createdAt`)

| Type | n (done) | median | p90 | min-max | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All real jobs | 47 first-try of 63 | 237 s | 404 s | 164-1269 s | mixed pre/post agent-bug fix |
| Plain VPS (Ubuntu etc.) | 18 | 207 s | 240 s | 164-266 s | **post-fix (10-02, N4, n=3): 163, 167, 167 s** |
| Game servers | 29 first-try (33 done) | 288 s | 442 s | 183-1269 s | |
| Minecraft | 9 | 252 s | 317 s | 209-353 s | post-fix N4: 251 s |
| Valheim | 9 | 404 s | 555 s | 197-579 s | N4 10-01: 395 s |
| Terraria | 4 | 258 s | 288 s | 183-288 s | N5 10-02: 285 s |
| Core Keeper | 2 | 257 s | 328 s | | N5 10-02: 255 s |
| Palworld | 2 | 293 s (and 1 job needed 2 attempts, 1177 s) | | | |
| Project Zomboid | 1 first-try | 372 s | | | the 10-02 retries both failed (RCA) |
| ARK | 1 | 1269 s | | | 22.9 GB SteamCMD download |
| Rust | 2, both needed retries | 1015-1475 s | | | |
| CS2 | 0 of 1 | failed at 2062 s | | | 66-71 GB install, known unsellable |

By node (first-try median): N2 228 s, N4 221 s, N1 220 s, N5 258 s, N3 266 s. No node is dramatically slower; N5 is slowest here only because it has had the heaviest mix (and its first-boot is the same stock path).

Queue wait is not a problem: `startedAt - createdAt` median 2 s (the 1227 s p90 is the post-outage re-queue of 10-01; `WORKER_CONCURRENCY` default is 8 with 16 slots).

### 2.2 Success, retry and failure reasons

- Real jobs: **51 done, 12 failed (19%)**; 47 of 63 (75%) succeeded on the first attempt; 16 jobs (25%) needed more than one attempt. Plain VPS: 18 of 19 first-try. Games: 29 of 44 first-try (66%).
- The 12 real failures: 4 DB unique-constraint on 09-06 (fixed code bug), 2 duplicate-private-IP incident (valheim N2, RCA), 2 blank PZ admin user (RCA), 1 CS2 (unsellable size), 1 Node.js template PVE 400 parameter error, 2 Minecraft "game port never opened" (09-06 N2 EHOSTUNREACH; 10-01 N5 during the sweep).
- Across all 69 failed jobs (including the sweep): 40 "game port never opened" (the 300 s window plus the install-progress heuristics), 5 "SSH did not respond" (N3 dedicated-IP orders, ~245 s), 4 "could not sync the game port forward on node-5" (NAT sync failure is fatal in `provision()`), 4 DB unique, 3 "VM already running", 1 worker restart.
- So failures are overwhelmingly bugs or oversized games, now mostly fixed, but **the retry cost is brutal**: a failing family burns 3 x (300 s port window + extended wait) = 16-35 minutes before the customer is told.

### 2.3 Where the time goes, derived timeline (4 clean post-fix provisions, 10-02)

Markers: claim; first NAT-sync burst (just before `qm start`); second burst (start of the game-port stage, i.e. after SSH + login + identity checks); third burst (immediately after the game port opened); DONE.

| Job | claim to start | start to guest verified | game stage (until port open) | tail (readiness, email, DNS job) | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ubuntu VPS, N4 (x3) | ~14 s | **148-151 s** | n/a | ~3 s | 163-167 s |
| Minecraft, N4 | ~14 s | **148 s** | 77 s | 12 s | 251 s |
| Terraria, N5 | ~18 s | **114 s** | 147 s | 6 s | 285 s |
| Core Keeper, N5 | ~18 s | **112 s** | 119 s | 6 s | 255 s |
| 10-01 sweep (N5, 20 clean samples, mixed families) | 11-19 s | median ~125 s (111-164) | 77-185 s | | |

Proxmox side, from node task logs (last 60 days): `qmclone` of the stock 9000 template median **8 s** (N1 9, N2 8 with p90 17 / max 67, N3 5, N4 8, N5 8, p90 16), `qmconfig` + `resize` ~0-1 s each, `qmstart` median 1-3 s. Pre-start work in the worker adds ~10 s: IP/ARP inventory ~4 s (N5 16:53:57 to 16:54:01), snippet write via node-agent ~2 s, NAT sync of all 5 nodes ~2-3 s. **The Proxmox/worker side is ~15-18 s of a 165-285 s provision. 85-90% of the time is inside the guest after boot.**

In-guest (from `DOCUMENTATION.md`, measured on stock Ubuntu 24.04 on N5, and `perf-guest-and-games.md`): sshd answers at ~23 s; cloud-init `package_update` + `qemu-guest-agent` + `unzip` takes **72.2 s** (`config-package_update_upgrade_install`); `cloud-final` takes 82-132 s in total on stock guests; the agent is only up at ~95 s because the stock template **does not contain the agent** (the platform waits for something that cloud-init has to apt-install first); `get.docker.com` + a 345 MB pull + `docker create` ~25 s (more on slower mirrors; the Terraria and Core Keeper game stages of 119-147 s suggest the real figure on N5 is much larger than 25 s, but I cannot split docker install from game init without R0); Minecraft world generation ~30-35 s.

Unexplained residual: a plain Ubuntu VPS takes 148-151 s after start although agent-up is at ~95 s. I cannot attribute the extra ~50 s with the data available (candidates: slower boot on N4 under memory pressure, the three sequential SSH sessions for login/identity/key install, SSH 5 s polling). R0 would resolve it.

Polling windows are not a problem: guest agent polled every 2 s, SSH every 5 s, game port every 10 s (rechecked every 10 s inside the extended wait as well, so a port that opens mid-minute is caught within 10 s). They cost 5-10 s on average, not minutes.

---

## 3. Biggest time sinks and fragility (ranked)

1. **The stock template has no guest agent and runs `package_update` on every first boot: 72 s on every provision, including every plain VPS.** `chooseCloneSource` (lib/golden-template.ts) only allows a baked template for game orders, so plain VPS orders (27% of real jobs) always pay it. This is the single biggest controllable item.
2. **`curl get.docker.com | sh` on every game VM** (apt update, ~7 packages, reinstall on every VM). Retried 3x now (good) but still a WAN dependency per VM, ~25-60 s, plus a failure source.
3. **`docker pull` on every VM, direct from Docker Hub, `:latest` tags.** Compressed sizes measured from the registry today: itzg/minecraft-server 345 MB (java21) / 355 MB (java25), lloesche/valheim-server 372 MB, didstopia/rust-server 379 MB, thijsvanloef/palworld 382 MB, hermsi/ark-server 294 MB, ryshe/terraria 220 MB, core-keeper 285 MB, mornedhels/enshrouded 734 MB, sknnr/ark-ascended 716 MB, **joedwards32/cs2 1239 MB**, ich777/steamcmd:dayz 50 MB, cm2network/tf2 152 MB. The repo's brief expectation of "multi-GB images" is wrong for most families: images are 0.15-1.2 GB. The multi-GB cost is the **game files** (next item). Of 62 active catalog families, ~59 pull from Docker Hub and 3 from ghcr.io (abioticfactor, gmod, theisle): a Docker `registry-mirrors` setting does **not** cover ghcr.io.
   - N2/N3/N4/N5 are NAT islands: every VM on a node shares one public egress IP, hence one anonymous Docker Hub budget. The 10-02 valheim incident's killed pull was attributed (inferred, not proven) to this plus a duplicate IP.
4. **Steam game files downloaded per server, from Steam, at first container start.** Real sizes (docs + `perf-guest-and-games.md`): Valheim 2.1 GB, PZ 6.9 GB, ARK 22.9 GB, Squad 21.4 GB, Stationeers 12.3 GB, CS2 66-71 GB. Nothing is shared between servers, even on the same node. The Valheim image also runs `steamcmd validate` every 15 minutes (`UPDATE_CRON`).
5. **Failure cost model:** 300 s base port window, then up to 45 min of "still installing" heuristics, times 3 attempts. Already improved on 10-02 (crash-loop/fatal detection, idempotent re-run). No further structural issue, but the retry multiplier makes every install-time problem 3x as visible.
6. **NAT sync is a full 5-node verify, run 3x per non-primary provision** (pre-start, game-port, join-ports; ~2-3 s each) plus 2 follow-up jobs (`SYNC_FORWARDS`, `SYNC_GAME_DNS`) after. It is also **fatal** in the game-port step (4 observed failures on N5). Small in time, relevant in fragility.
7. **Template drift** (section 4.4): different base-image dates per node, templates missing on 3 of 5 nodes.
8. **No digest pinning**: the same `:latest` can resolve differently per node and per day; a provision after an upstream release can break the first-boot of one node only.
9. **Claude CLI install and telemetry shipper download run after the game** (fixed 10-01), but they still compete for CPU/network with game start on small plans. Minor.
10. **Single 1 Gb uplink on N1-N4** (N5 has 10 Gb): concurrent Steam installs (8-70 GB) on one node saturate it, which also hurts running customers. (Source: `perf-hypervisor.md` NIC table.)

---

## 4. Design options

### 4.1 Golden templates with Docker preinstalled and images pre-pulled (extends what exists)

State today: `scripts/golden/build-golden-template.sh` + `lib/golden-template.ts` implement it; node N2 holds a POC template **9101** (tag `nxeon-golden`, virtual 12 G, 4.24 GB referenced, images itzg/minecraft-server java21+java25 + lloesche/valheim-server, built 2026-10-01). **Not used in production**: `NXEON_GOLDEN_GAME_TEMPLATE` and `NXEON_GOLDEN_LINKED_CLONE` are unset in the live worker process (checked via its environment) and not in `.env`. No other node has a golden template.

Measured on N2 (docs + `qmclone` task log): full clone of golden 63-67 s (stock 9000: 13-25 s), **linked clone 1-2 s**; golden guest-agent ~15 s; docker +1.2 s.

Problems with the current implementation that I would fix before enabling:
- **Virtual size 12 G.** `chooseCloneSource` refuses the golden clone when the template disk is larger than the order's disk (a resize cannot shrink). Game plans with min disk below 12 G exist: bedrock 5 G, cs16 8 G, necesse 8 G, and 10 G for ats, ets2, barotrauma, dst, factorio, unturned, vintagestory. Rebuild at 9-10 G (4.2 GB used); orders at 5-8 G keep the stock path.
- **One platform-wide vmid in an env var**, while rollout is per node. A rebuild must get a brand-new vmid (never-reuse rule), so flipping the env requires the same new vmid to exist on every node first. Move the mapping to the DB per node (family, vmid, version, builtAt, image digests). Then one node can run v2 while others run v1.
- **Plain VPS cannot use it** (`isGame` gate). Two flavours are needed: `base` (agent, unzip, curl, git, ca-certs; for VPS) and `game-base` (plus Docker CE, no per-game images or a small common set). Docker preinstalled on a plain VPS would be a product change (a running dockerd, iptables chains) so keep it out of the VPS flavour.
- **Pre-pulled images live on every full clone's disk** (4.24 GB used vs 1-1.75 GB stock). With linked clones this costs nothing (shared blocks); with full clones it eats plan disk. So: linked clones, or few images.
- **Image set**: Minecraft (31% of recent game orders; two Java variants), Valheim, Terraria, Core Keeper, Palworld, Rust, PZ, bedrock, DST, CS2 is too large. About 8 images x ~350 MB = ~3 GB. Add by order volume (60-day orders: minecraft 9, valheim 6, terraria 3, rust 2, bedrock 2, palworld 2, PZ 2, core keeper 2, ark 1, dst 1, cs2 1).

Expected effect (R1+R2 together): guest verified at ~45 s from claim instead of 112-148 s; Minecraft ~100-120 s (from 251), Terraria/Core Keeper ~100-120 s (from 255-285), Ubuntu VPS ~60-75 s (from 165). These totals are **estimates**; the components (agent 15 s, docker +1.2 s, linked clone 2 s, 72 s package step) are measured.

### 4.2 Node-local read-through registry cache (+ Docker Hub account)

The repo has the client half (`NXEON_DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR`, `registryMirrorPrelude`, opt-in, only applies to a guest with no Docker yet; design in the RCA). Missing: the cache itself, the per-node setting, and pre-warm.

Recommended shape:
- `registry:2` in proxy mode (`REGISTRY_PROXY_REMOTEURL=https://registry-1.docker.io`, with a Docker Hub account token so the *cache* pulls at the authenticated limit) bound to each node's vmbr1 gateway only (10.20.N.1:5000; the primary's is 10.20.0.1). Guests reach it without leaving the node; one WAN pull per layer per node.
- **Set `proxy.ttl` low** (default is 168 h, so `:latest` could be a week stale), or better, pin digests in the catalog (R3). The platform records no digest today.
- **ghcr.io images (3 families) are not covered by `registry-mirrors`**; they need a containerd `hosts.toml` mirror or a rewritten image reference.
- A per-node cache beats a single cache on the primary: a primary-hosted cache would push N2/N5 guests over the public internet to Singapore, slower than Docker Hub's CDN.
- With golden templates (4.1) the cache matters less for the top families, but it covers the long tail (~50 other families) and removes the rate-limit failure class. It also supports `docker pull` on reinstall/update jobs.
- Disk: ~20-40 GB on `/tank` or NVMe per node. Risk: low (client falls back to Hub).

Expected gain: 10-60 s on the first pull of a family on a node; later pulls at LAN speed. Honest note: at the current volume (a family lands on a given node a few times per month) a lot of pulls will still be first pulls, so the **pre-warm** step (pull the whole catalog through the cache after a catalog change) is what makes it pay.

### 4.3 Steam game-file caching: lancache vs ZFS-clone game templates

| Option | How | Speed | Hit rate at *this* volume | Cost / risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Lancache-style HTTP cache per node (DNS-override of Steam CDN hostnames to a node-local nginx cache) | All Steam families at once, no per-game work | LAN speed on a hit; a miss is a normal download | **Poor**: ~13 Steam-family orders in 60 days across 5 nodes means almost every install is a first install on that node | Needs guest DNS to point at a node-local resolver (cloud-init sets `1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8` today), 100-300 GB cache disk, cache poisoning surface |
| B. Game-file template (linked clone of a VM with `/opt/<game>` pre-installed) | Build once per family per node; `qm clone --full 0` | Install becomes a delta/validate: seconds to a couple of minutes | **100% regardless of volume** | Disk per family per node (Valheim 2.1, PZ 6.9, Rust ~8-10, Palworld ~5-8, ARK 22.9 GB; ~50 GB for 5 families, fits N5/N3/N2, **not N4 or N1** which are at 65-68% pool use); stale after game patches so rebuild weekly (steam validate on start brings the delta); template must contain **no** per-server state or secrets |
| C. Do nothing, only raise the port-wait budget | | none | n/a | status quo |

Recommendation: **B for the 4-5 families that have actual customers and long installs** (Valheim, PZ, Rust, Palworld, ARK), A only if Steam volume grows by an order of magnitude. Implementation notes: build the template by running the real catalog setup script with dummy secrets, stop the container before it writes a world, `rm` configs/worlds/passwords, power off, template. Per-server env (`SERVER_PASS`, RCON, ADMIN) is applied at `docker create`, so nothing server-specific lives on disk beforehand; verify with `scripts/verify-game-provision.ts` after a canary order. Linked clones and `zfs send`-based VM moves (`docs/VM-MOVE.md` uses `zfs send -L -e` of the VM's own dataset): a send of a clone should transmit full data (flatten), but **this must be tested on a scratch VM before relying on it**, I did not verify it.

### 4.4 Template consistency across non-clustered nodes: current drift (measured)

| | 9000 | other templates | golden |
|---|---|---|---|
| N1 primary | built 2026-07-23 | 9000-9009 all present (+ coldemail-relay 9010, a running VM in the template range) | none |
| N2 | 2026-09-05 | 9000-9004 only | 9101 (POC) |
| N3 | 2026-09-10 | 9000-9009 | none |
| N4 | 2026-09-16 | 9000-9004 only | none |
| N5 | 2026-09-29 | 9000, 9002-9004 (**no 9001 Debian 13**) | none |

- Every node's `base-9000-disk-0@__base__` snapshot has a **different ZFS guid** (e.g. 12185958301651175407 on N1 vs 14929693755408565516 on N2), because templates were restored from vzdump archives (`scripts/onboard-node.sh`, `export-templates.sh`) or rebuilt. Their **content is not guaranteed identical**; the N1 base image is 71 days old, N5's is 3 days old (kernel, cloud-init and package versions differ per node).
- N2 stores the 9000 config with `cicustom ...vmdata-hdd:snippets/...` while others use `backup:`; benign (storage alias), the only config difference. `nxeon-vendor.yaml` is byte-identical on all five (md5 a7b21b71...).
- The scheduler already excludes nodes lacking a template (`nodesWithTemplate`), but only checks *presence by vmid*, not content or age.
- Proposal (R8): a per-node `TemplateRecord` table; build each template **once** on a build node and `zfs send | zstd | ssh zfs recv` the `@__base__` snapshot to the other nodes, then write the matching `qemu-server/<vmid>.conf` (a 1.75-4 GB transfer, a minute or two). Then the ZFS guid is identical everywhere and **drift detection is a one-line comparison of guids** (plus config hash and vendor-yaml md5) in a read-only sweep, run daily and shown in /admin. Pin the version on the server (`Server.templateVmid`) so reinstalls use the same source. Running servers are never affected by a template update: a full clone is independent, and a linked clone depends on the *specific old snapshot*, which is why a rebuild must get a new vmid and the old template stays until its last clone is gone (already documented in `golden-template.ts`).

### 4.5 Warm pool

Pre-provisioned VMs per popular plan and region, claimed at order time.

- **Stopped** pool entries (cloned, images preloaded): claim = set config + start, ~30-45 s to ready. After R1/R2 a cold provision is already ~60-120 s, so the gain is ~20-40 s.
- **Running** pool entries: claim in 5-10 s, but each idles pinned RAM (a 4 GB Minecraft shell x 2 per region = 8 GB, ~15% of one node, in regions that are already RAM-constrained) and needs per-claim re-keying (root password via guest agent, management key, SSH host keys, hostname, telemetry token, game env, correct memory/cores, IP/port already allocated in IPAM for the pool slot).
- Verdict: **not worth it before R1/R2**; revisit only for plain Ubuntu and Minecraft with real demand data. Capacity is the binding constraint, not clone time.

### 4.6 Parallelising independent steps (R6)

Safe candidates, each small:
- IP/ARP inventory (~4 s) and clone (5-8 s) run in parallel (IP is only needed for config).
- Allocate game and join-port forwards **before** `qm start` (ports are known from the family), sync NAT **once**, and drop the 2 later full 5-node syncs from the critical path (saves ~5 s and removes a fatal failure mode seen 4x on N5). Sync only the target node, not all five.
- Merge `ensureGuestAccess` + `verifyGuestIdentity` + `installManagementKey` + the first startup sample into one SSH session.
- SSH poll 5 s to 2 s; TCP game-port poll 10 s to 3 s.
- `runProvisionReadiness` (6-12 s tail) and the deployment email in parallel.
Total ~15-25 s. Low individual value; do after R1/R2.

### 4.7 Other items worth doing

- **iothread/ssd on `scsi0` in the template config** (new provisions inherit): `perf-hypervisor.md` P1-1. Free for new VMs.
- **`compression=lz4` on the `data` pools** of N1/N3/N4/N5 (off today; N2 on): new blocks only; also shrinks templates 1.4-1.7x as seen on N2 (9000 is 1.00 GB there vs 1.75 GB elsewhere). P1-2 in the hypervisor report.
- **Pin image digests** after a verified provision (`scripts/verify-game-provision.ts` already prints them).
- **Stale-template refresh**: weekly rebuild of the base templates from the current Ubuntu cloud image (the package step no longer needs to run at first boot, so security patches must come from a fresh template, not from first-boot apt).

---

## 5. Capacity and placement as a performance factor (live numbers, 2026-10-02 17:46-18:00 UTC)

### 5.1 Current state per node

| | N1 primary (SGP) | N2 (FSN) | N3 (SGP) | N4 (SGP) | N5 (BHS) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Sum of running VM RAM ("ceiling") / physical | 66.0 GB = **103%** | 67.6 GB = **106%** | 28.7 GB = 90% (+8.5 GB ARC on 32 GB) | 77.8 GB = **122%** | 30.7 GB = 48% |

| Accepts new provisions (`acceptsProvisions`) | **no** | yes | **no** | yes | yes |

Notes and caveats:
- Steal time is not applicable (bare metal hosts, `steal` 0 in `/proc/stat`). The noisy-neighbour signal on these hosts is **host CPU PSI, run-queue and swap**, not steal: only N1 (and mildly N4) show CPU contention; N1 also runs the Nxeon app, Postgres and `next build` (see `docs/PRIMARY-OFFLOAD-PLAN.md`, still valid: load 20 on 8 threads at sampling time).
- "Guest memory in use" is the guest balloon stat; qemu RSS is larger (page cache, never-returned pages). With pinned RAM the host cost of a VM trends toward its full ceiling as the guest touches pages, which is why a 122% ceiling on N4 already produces full swap with 1.9 GB free.
- Ballooning: new VMs are pinned (`balloon = memory`, `NXEON_BALLOON_POLICY` default `pin`), but **17 running VMs still sit at the old 50% floor and are currently squeezed**, including N1 vm 105 (live Soul Pilates) at 5.6/8 GB. Re-pinning them without first adding capacity would push N3/N4/N1 into OOM. The `perf-hypervisor.md` P0-2 recommendation is right but must come **after** R7.
- "Germany/Canada have room" is only half true: **N5 (Canada) really has room** (47% committed, 25 GB free). **N2 (Germany) is also over-committed** by the platform's own accounting (120%, ceiling 106% of physical) although its real use (47%) and 14 GB free look comfortable. Capacity numbers in `Node.capacityRamMB` are also stale (N3 is a 32 GB box configured as 23.9 GB, which is conservative; N4 is a 64 GB box configured as 56 GB).
- `NXEON_RAM_GUARD` defaults to `warn` (log only) because enforcing it refused every Singapore order on 10-01; the scheduler's real rule is DB plan-RAM under 90% critical for strict (region-bound) placement. It is **RAM only: no CPU, no live PSI, no swap, no disk-overcommit, no template/cache locality.**

### 5.2 How oversubscribed, in sellable terms

Policy used by the existing guard: guaranteed RAM <= 0.95 x (physical - 10 GB host reserve) = 51.3 GB on a 64 GB node, 20.9 GB on N3.

| Node | Pinned/ceiling RAM now | Allowed | Over (GB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| N1 | 66.0 | 51.3 | +14.7 (includes ~15.7 GB of company VMs: mail, hosting, studio) |
| N2 | 67.6 | 51.3 | +16.3 |
| N3 | 28.7 | 20.9 | +7.8 |
| N4 | 77.8 | 51.3 | +26.5 |
| N5 | 30.7 | 51.3 | **-20.6 (headroom)** |

The fleet is **~65 GB over the policy line against ~21 GB of headroom, all of it in Canada**. In Singapore (the region taking ~61% of new orders, see below) there is **no** sellable headroom at all and nothing can be re-pinned. Real usage is only ~53% of paid RAM fleet-wide (142 of 270 GB), so the situation is not an imminent mass-OOM, but N4 (1.9 GB free, swap full) and N3 (3.3 GB free) are one burst away, and N1 already had an OOM kill of the mail VM on 2026-09-25 (per `perf-hypervisor.md`).

### 5.3 Demand (from the DB)

- 52 live servers, **44 created in the last 30 days**, 17 in the last 7. By region (30 d): Singapore 27 servers / 123 GB plan RAM, Germany 10 / 54 GB, Canada 7 / 26 GB. Singapore 7-day: 8 servers / 32 GB (~4.5 GB/day). At that rate **one 64 GB node's ~51 GB of sellable RAM lasts ~11-12 days in Singapore**. (Uncertainty: the window may include partner grants, tests and a launch spike; I did not separate them.)
- Order mix: games 33 of 44 (Minecraft first), plain VPS 11.

### 5.4 Recommended placement and overcommit policy

1. **No overcommit of pinned RAM for game servers.** Sum of guaranteed RAM <= 0.95 x (RAM - 12 GB) per node, enforced (`NXEON_RAM_GUARD=enforce`) once R7's new node exists; until then keep `warn` and rely on `acceptsProvisions=false` on full nodes. Never balloon a game VM below plan RAM.
2. **Optional measured overcommit for plain VPS only**, after a month of per-VM RSS data: idle VPS use 25-45% of RAM (e.g. VMs 102/104/108 etc. in the cap data), so a ceiling-to-physical ratio of up to ~1.15 could be defensible *if* free-page reporting is verified; do not do this on nodes with ARC starved or swap in use.
3. **Schedule on live signals, not just DB plan-RAM**: reject or penalise a node when MemAvailable < 10%, swap > 25% used, CPU PSI some avg300 > 15-20%, vCPU:thread > 3:1 (N1 4.0, N4 4.6 today), pool > 75% used (ZFS degrades past ~80%; N4 65% with 2.5x sold) or sold-virtual > 2x pool.
4. **Prefer a node that already holds the golden/game-file template and image cache** for the family, then most sellable headroom.
5. **Stop N1 taking customer load** (already `acceptsProvisions=false`; the offload plan stands). Keep N3 closed until its ARC (8.5 GB on 32 GB) is cut to ~3 GB and RAM is re-based (it is the weakest box: 32 GB).
6. Fix `Node.capacityRamMB` to physical RAM minus reserve per node so DB capacity and the guard agree; add per-node `capacityVcpu` (suggest <= 3:1 per thread for game nodes, as game servers are single-thread bound and N1/N4 show contention).

### 5.5 Capacity plan: when and what

Triggers to order a node (any one): sellable headroom in a region < 2 weeks of recent demand (Singapore today: **0 days, trigger already tripped**); host MemAvailable < 10% for 1 h; swap used > 25%; CPU PSI some avg300 > 20%; pool used > 75% or sold virtual > 2x; ARC cannot reach its target.

Spec: the existing boxes are RAM-bound, not CPU-bound (CPU PSI 0 everywhere except N1), and VM RAM is what is sold, so buy **RAM per node**: **12-16 threads, 128 GB ECC, 2 x NVMe >= 960 GB mirror (pools are 358-452 GB today and 2.0-2.5x sold on N1/N4), 10 GbE if offered (Steam installs, 1 Gb is shared by every simultaneous install)**. A 128 GB node sells ~108 GB (0.95 x (128-12)... conservative 100 GB), i.e. ~3 weeks of Singapore demand at the recent rate. Order **two Singapore nodes** (one is already needed to un-squeeze N1/N3/N4 and re-pin 17 VMs; the second covers growth and gives N+1 so a node can be drained for maintenance). Cost reference from the DB: current nodes cost $33-78/month each (`monthlyCostCents`); I have no price for a 128 GB class, so no cost claim. Order lead time is the risk: place the order before the next campaign, not after.

Other capacity-adjacent findings worth flagging: N5's `backup`/`vmdata-hdd` is a **20 GB directory at 90.7% used** (backups for node-5 servers will fail soon); N2's NVMe pair and N5's second NVMe have high wear per `perf-hypervisor.md`; N1 root disk was 98% full on 10-01 (Postgres crash 09-27).

---

## 6. Rollout, canary and measurement

Common rule: **N5 is the canary node** (healthy, 10 Gb, 47% committed, accepts provisions), then N3/N2, then N4. Template presence per node is already the natural per-node switch (`chooseCloneSource` falls back to stock if the template is missing), which gives instant rollback (untag or remove the template; no deploy).

| Step | Do | Verify | Roll back |
|---|---|---|---|
| R0 | Add `Job.phases`; record: claimed, inventory done, clone done, config done, started, agent up, ssh up, login ok, game stage start, port open, readiness done, DONE; add `Server.cloneSource` (vmid, golden flag) | 10 real provisions show all marks; admin table of p50/p90 per family/node/cloneSource | Column is additive; ignore it |
| R1 | Build `base` Ubuntu 24.04 template on N5 (new vmid in 9100-9199, run the existing build script with no images); allow `chooseCloneSource` for non-game Ubuntu 24.04 | 5 canary VPS orders on N5: agent up <= 25 s, total <= 90 s; SSH login, password and management key work; `cloud-init status` clean; no `package_update` in the log | Remove the template from N5 |
| R2 | Rebuild `game-base` at 9-10 G with the top image set; set `NXEON_GOLDEN_GAME_TEMPLATE` + `NXEON_GOLDEN_LINKED_CLONE=1` (or the DB mapping); N5 only | 5 Minecraft + 3 Terraria/Core Keeper + 2 Valheim on N5; `scripts/verify-game-provision.ts` `CLEAN BILL OF HEALTH`; compare p50 with the baselines in 2.1/2.3; test a **backup, restore and VM move of a linked-clone server** on a scratch VM before opening it to customers | Unset env / remove template; existing servers are unaffected (their disks are independent or tied only to their own old template snapshot) |
| R3 | Run `registry:2` proxy on N2 first; per-node mirror setting | A provision on N2 shows pulls hitting the cache (cache logs); a stopped cache still provisions | Clear the mirror setting |
| R4 | One family at a time (Valheim first, highest volume among Steam families) on N5 | Install time and `verify-game-provision` identical to a cold install; no world/secret in the template (diff the template's `/opt` against a clean image) | Remove template |
| R7 | Order nodes; onboard with `scripts/onboard-node.sh` (it already sets ARC cap, firewall, agent, templates from archives); then re-pin the 17 squeezed VMs and flip `NXEON_RAM_GUARD=enforce` | MemAvailable, swap, CPU PSI per node before/after | n/a |

Metrics to track from R0 on (per family and per node): p50/p90 claim-to-RUNNING, first-attempt success rate, % of jobs needing a retry, and the per-phase table; node-side: MemAvailable, swap used, CPU PSI avg300, pool %, sold-virtual ratio. Success criteria: plain VPS p50 <= 75 s, Minecraft/Terraria/Core Keeper p50 <= 120 s, first-attempt success >= 90% on games, 0 customer VMs below plan RAM.

---

## 7. Uncertainty and what I did not verify

- Phase split inside the guest is inferred, not measured on these runs (no per-phase data exists). The ~50 s unexplained gap on plain Ubuntu (148-151 s from start vs ~95 s to agent-up) and the 119-147 s game stages for Terraria/Core Keeper are open until R0 exists.
- All "expected gains" for R2/R4/R6 are estimates built from measured components; only the golden POC's agent time (15 s), docker (+1.2 s) and linked clone (2.1 s) were measured, once, on N2.
- I did not run or time any provision, any clone, any `docker pull` or any Steam download; registry sizes are compressed layer sums from the Docker Hub API (amd64), not measured pull speeds. Steam install sizes are taken from the repo's docs and the sibling report.
- Linked-clone behaviour with `vzdump`, `zfs send` VM moves and `qmrestore` is reasoned from the docs/code, **not tested**.
- Whether `registry-mirrors` plus `proxy.ttl` behaves as described for `:latest` tags is from registry documentation, not tested here.
- Capacity: one snapshot at ~17:50 UTC on a Friday; no time series, no peak-hour data. The demand rate may include partner grants and tests.
- The 122 jobs without a live server were treated as test/sweep/deleted, based on the 10-01 sweep dates and error text; I did not read their server rows (deleted).
- No customer data was read; guest-internal timings for customer VMs were not collected by me (I used the existing docs and the sibling report instead).

Date: 2026-10-02. Strictly read-only (repo, SELECT-only DB scripts, read-only SSH/pvesh on the 5 nodes, `journalctl` on the worker, public Docker registry metadata). ## 0. Evidence quality, read this first

- **There is no per-phase timing stored anywhere.** `Job` keeps createdAt/startedAt/finishedAt and only the *last* step label (`Job.step`, `Server.provisioningStep`). `startedAt` only exists for jobs since 2026-10-01 (54 of 185 PROVISION rows). So "time per phase" below is **derived** from three independent sources: (a) worker journald markers (claim, snippet write, the three NAT-sync bursts, DONE), (b) Proxmox task logs on the nodes (clone/config/start durations), (c) in-guest numbers already measured in `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` and `perf-guest-and-games.md`. Phases inside the guest (cloud-init package step, docker install, pull, game init) are **not separable from the DB**; they are inferred. Roadmap item R0 fixes this.
- Durations before 2026-10-01 contain the old guest-agent bug (a fixed 180 s wait on every provision, fixed 10-01). I use post-fix runs (10-02) for the baseline and say so.
- 122 of the 185 PROVISION rows have no surviving Server row. 81 of those are the 2026-10-01 all-families catalog sweep (test servers on N5, queue-delayed, many deliberately huge or broken games). They are excluded from production-like statistics. 63 jobs have a live Server row ("real").
- Order volume is small (44 new servers in 30 days, 17 in the last 7), so per-family/per-node cells have n of 1 to 15. Medians for n<5 are anecdotes.

### 2.2 Success, retry and failure reasons

- Real jobs: **51 done, 12 failed (19%)**; 47 of 63 (75%) succeeded on the first attempt; 16 jobs (25%) needed more than one attempt. Plain VPS: 18 of 19 first-try. Games: 29 of 44 first-try (66%).
- The 12 real failures: 4 DB unique-constraint on 09-06 (fixed code bug), 2 duplicate-private-IP incident (valheim N2, RCA), 2 blank PZ admin user (RCA), 1 CS2 (unsellable size), 1 Node.js template PVE 400 parameter error, 2 Minecraft "game port never opened" (09-06 N2 EHOSTUNREACH; 10-01 N5 during the sweep).
- Across all 69 failed jobs (including the sweep): 40 "game port never opened" (the 300 s window plus the install-progress heuristics), 5 "SSH did not respond" (N3 dedicated-IP orders, ~245 s), 4 "could not sync the game port forward on node-5" (NAT sync failure is fatal in `provision()`), 4 DB unique, 3 "VM already running", 1 worker restart.
- So failures are overwhelmingly bugs or oversized games, now mostly fixed, but **the retry cost is brutal**: a failing family burns 3 x (300 s port window + extended wait) = 16-35 minutes before the customer is told.

In-guest (from `DOCUMENTATION.md`, measured on stock Ubuntu 24.04 on N5, and `perf-guest-and-games.md`): sshd answers at ~23 s; cloud-init `package_update` + `qemu-guest-agent` + `unzip` takes **72.2 s** (`config-package_update_upgrade_install`); `cloud-final` takes 82-132 s in total on stock guests; the agent is only up at ~95 s because the stock template **does not contain the agent** (the platform waits for something that cloud-init has to apt-install first); `get.docker.com` + a 345 MB pull + `docker create` ~25 s (more on slower mirrors; the Terraria and Core Keeper game stages of 119-147 s suggest the real figure on N5 is much larger than 25 s, but I cannot split docker install from game init without R0); Minecraft world generation ~30-35 s.

R0 would resolve it.

Polling windows are not a problem: guest agent polled every 2 s, SSH every 5 s, game port every 10 s (rechecked every 10 s inside the extended wait as well, so a port that opens mid-minute is caught within 10 s). They cost 5-10 s on average, not minutes.

## 3. Biggest time sinks and fragility (ranked)

1. **The stock template has no guest agent and runs `package_update` on every first boot: 72 s on every provision, including every plain VPS.** `chooseCloneSource` (lib/golden-template.ts) only allows a baked template for game orders, so plain VPS orders (27% of real jobs) always pay it. This is the single biggest controllable item.
2. **`curl get.docker.com | sh` on every game VM** (apt update, ~7 packages, reinstall on every VM). Retried 3x now (good) but still a WAN dependency per VM, ~25-60 s, plus a failure source.
3. **`docker pull` on every VM, direct from Docker Hub, `:latest` tags.** Compressed sizes measured from the registry today: itzg/minecraft-server 345 MB (java21) / 355 MB (java25), lloesche/valheim-server 372 MB, didstopia/rust-server 379 MB, thijsvanloef/palworld 382 MB, hermsi/ark-server 294 MB, ryshe/terraria 220 MB, core-keeper 285 MB, mornedhels/enshrouded 734 MB, sknnr/ark-ascended 716 MB, **joedwards32/cs2 1239 MB**, ich777/steamcmd:dayz 50 MB, cm2network/tf2 152 MB. The repo's brief expectation of "multi-GB images" is wrong for most families: images are 0.15-1.2 GB. The multi-GB cost is the **game files** (next item). Of 62 active catalog families, ~59 pull from Docker Hub and 3 from ghcr.io (abioticfactor, gmod, theisle): a Docker `registry-mirrors` setting does **not** cover ghcr.io.
   - N2/N3/N4/N5 are NAT islands: every VM on a node shares one public egress IP, hence one anonymous Docker Hub budget. The 10-02 valheim incident's killed pull was attributed (inferred, not proven) to this plus a duplicate IP.
4. **Steam game files downloaded per server, from Steam, at first container start.** Real sizes (docs + `perf-guest-and-games.md`): Valheim 2.1 GB, PZ 6.9 GB, ARK 22.9 GB, Squad 21.4 GB, Stationeers 12.3 GB, CS2 66-71 GB. Nothing is shared between servers, even on the same node. The Valheim image also runs `steamcmd validate` every 15 minutes (`UPDATE_CRON`).
5. **Failure cost model:** 300 s base port window, then up to 45 min of "still installing" heuristics, times 3 attempts. Already improved on 10-02 (crash-loop/fatal detection, idempotent re-run). No further structural issue, but the retry multiplier makes every install-time problem 3x as visible.
6. **NAT sync is a full 5-node verify, run 3x per non-primary provision** (pre-start, game-port, join-ports; ~2-3 s each) plus 2 follow-up jobs (`SYNC_FORWARDS`, `SYNC_GAME_DNS`) after. It is also **fatal** in the game-port step (4 observed failures on N5). Small in time, relevant in fragility.
7. **Template drift** (section 4.4): different base-image dates per node, templates missing on 3 of 5 nodes.
8. **No digest pinning**: the same `:latest` can resolve differently per node and per day; a provision after an upstream release can break the first-boot of one node only.
9. **Claude CLI install and telemetry shipper download run after the game** (fixed 10-01), but they still compete for CPU/network with game start on small plans. Minor.
10. **Single 1 Gb uplink on N1-N4** (N5 has 10 Gb): concurrent Steam installs (8-70 GB) on one node saturate it, which also hurts running customers. (Source: `perf-hypervisor.md` NIC table.)

## 4. Design options

### 4.1 Golden templates with Docker preinstalled and images pre-pulled (extends what exists)

State today: `scripts/golden/build-golden-template.sh` + `lib/golden-template.ts` implement it; node N2 holds a POC template **9101** (tag `nxeon-golden`, virtual 12 G, 4.24 GB referenced, images itzg/minecraft-server java21+java25 + lloesche/valheim-server, built 2026-10-01). **Not used in production**: `NXEON_GOLDEN_GAME_TEMPLATE` and `NXEON_GOLDEN_LINKED_CLONE` are unset in the live worker process (checked via its environment) and not in `.env`. No other node has a golden template.

Measured on N2 (docs + `qmclone` task log): full clone of golden 63-67 s (stock 9000: 13-25 s), **linked clone 1-2 s**; golden guest-agent ~15 s; docker +1.2 s.

Problems with the current implementation that I would fix before enabling:
- **Virtual size 12 G.** `chooseCloneSource` refuses the golden clone when the template disk is larger than the order's disk (a resize cannot shrink). Game plans with min disk below 12 G exist: bedrock 5 G, cs16 8 G, necesse 8 G, and 10 G for ats, ets2, barotrauma, dst, factorio, unturned, vintagestory. Rebuild at 9-10 G (4.2 GB used); orders at 5-8 G keep the stock path.
- **One platform-wide vmid in an env var**, while rollout is per node. A rebuild must get a brand-new vmid (never-reuse rule), so flipping the env requires the same new vmid to exist on every node first. Move the mapping to the DB per node (family, vmid, version, builtAt, image digests). Then one node can run v2 while others run v1.
- **Plain VPS cannot use it** (`isGame` gate). Two flavours are needed: `base` (agent, unzip, curl, git, ca-certs; for VPS) and `game-base` (plus Docker CE, no per-game images or a small common set). Docker preinstalled on a plain VPS would be a product change (a running dockerd, iptables chains) so keep it out of the VPS flavour.
- **Pre-pulled images live on every full clone's disk** (4.24 GB used vs 1-1.75 GB stock). With linked clones this costs nothing (shared blocks); with full clones it eats plan disk. So: linked clones, or few images.
- **Image set**: Minecraft (31% of recent game orders; two Java variants), Valheim, Terraria, Core Keeper, Palworld, Rust, PZ, bedrock, DST, CS2 is too large. About 8 images x ~350 MB = ~3 GB. Add by order volume (60-day orders: minecraft 9, valheim 6, terraria 3, rust 2, bedrock 2, palworld 2, PZ 2, core keeper 2, ark 1, dst 1, cs2 1).

Expected effect (R1+R2 together): guest verified at ~45 s from claim instead of 112-148 s; Minecraft ~100-120 s (from 251), Terraria/Core Keeper ~100-120 s (from 255-285), Ubuntu VPS ~60-75 s (from 165). These totals are **estimates**; the components (agent 15 s, docker +1.2 s, linked clone 2 s, 72 s package step) are measured.

### 4.2 Node-local read-through registry cache (+ Docker Hub account)

The repo has the client half (`NXEON_DOCKER_REGISTRY_MIRROR`, `registryMirrorPrelude`, opt-in, only applies to a guest with no Docker yet; design in the RCA). Missing: the cache itself, the per-node setting, and pre-warm.

Recommended shape:
- `registry:2` in proxy mode (`REGISTRY_PROXY_REMOTEURL=https://registry-1.docker.io`, with a Docker Hub account token so the *cache* pulls at the authenticated limit) bound to each node's vmbr1 gateway only (10.20.N.1:5000; the primary's is 10.20.0.1). Guests reach it without leaving the node; one WAN pull per layer per node.
- **Set `proxy.ttl` low** (default is 168 h, so `:latest` could be a week stale), or better, pin digests in the catalog (R3). The platform records no digest today.
- **ghcr.io images (3 families) are not covered by `registry-mirrors`**; they need a containerd `hosts.toml` mirror or a rewritten image reference.
- A per-node cache beats a single cache on the primary: a primary-hosted cache would push N2/N5 guests over the public internet to Singapore, slower than Docker Hub's CDN.
- With golden templates (4.1) the cache matters less for the top families, but it covers the long tail (~50 other families) and removes the rate-limit failure class. It also supports `docker pull` on reinstall/update jobs.
- Disk: ~20-40 GB on `/tank` or NVMe per node. Risk: low (client falls back to Hub).

Expected gain: 10-60 s on the first pull of a family on a node; later pulls at LAN speed. Honest note: at the current volume (a family lands on a given node a few times per month) a lot of pulls will still be first pulls, so the **pre-warm** step (pull the whole catalog through the cache after a catalog change) is what makes it pay.

### 4.3 Steam game-file caching: lancache vs ZFS-clone game templates

| Option | How | Speed | Hit rate at *this* volume | Cost / risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Lancache-style HTTP cache per node (DNS-override of Steam CDN hostnames to a node-local nginx cache) | All Steam families at once, no per-game work | LAN speed on a hit; a miss is a normal download | **Poor**: ~13 Steam-family orders in 60 days across 5 nodes means almost every install is a first install on that node | Needs guest DNS to point at a node-local resolver (cloud-init sets `1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8` today), 100-300 GB cache disk, cache poisoning surface |
| B. Game-file template (linked clone of a VM with `/opt/<game>` pre-installed) | Build once per family per node; `qm clone --full 0` | Install becomes a delta/validate: seconds to a couple of minutes | **100% regardless of volume** | Disk per family per node (Valheim 2.1, PZ 6.9, Rust ~8-10, Palworld ~5-8, ARK 22.9 GB; ~50 GB for 5 families, fits N5/N3/N2, **not N4 or N1** which are at 65-68% pool use); stale after game patches so rebuild weekly (steam validate on start brings the delta); template must contain **no** per-server state or secrets |
| C. Do nothing, only raise the port-wait budget | | none | n/a | status quo |

Recommendation: **B for the 4-5 families that have actual customers and long installs** (Valheim, PZ, Rust, Palworld, ARK), A only if Steam volume grows by an order of magnitude. Implementation notes: build the template by running the real catalog setup script with dummy secrets, stop the container before it writes a world, `rm` configs/worlds/passwords, power off, template. Per-server env (`SERVER_PASS`, RCON, ADMIN) is applied at `docker create`, so nothing server-specific lives on disk beforehand; verify with `scripts/verify-game-provision.ts` after a canary order. Linked clones and `zfs send`-based VM moves (`docs/VM-MOVE.md` uses `zfs send -L -e` of the VM's own dataset): a send of a clone should transmit full data (flatten), but **this must be tested on a scratch VM before relying on it**, I did not verify it.

### 4.4 Template consistency across non-clustered nodes: current drift (measured)

| | 9000 | other templates | golden |
|---|---|---|---|
| N1 primary | built 2026-07-23 | 9000-9009 all present (+ coldemail-relay 9010, a running VM in the template range) | none |
| N2 | 2026-09-05 | 9000-9004 only | 9101 (POC) |
| N3 | 2026-09-10 | 9000-9009 | none |
| N4 | 2026-09-16 | 9000-9004 only | none |
| N5 | 2026-09-29 | 9000, 9002-9004 (**no 9001 Debian 13**) | none |

- Every node's `base-9000-disk-0@__base__` snapshot has a **different ZFS guid** (e.g. 12185958301651175407 on N1 vs 14929693755408565516 on N2), because templates were restored from vzdump archives (`scripts/onboard-node.sh`, `export-templates.sh`) or rebuilt. Their **content is not guaranteed identical**; the N1 base image is 71 days old, N5's is 3 days old (kernel, cloud-init and package versions differ per node).
- N2 stores the 9000 config with `cicustom ...vmdata-hdd:snippets/...` while others use `backup:`; benign (storage alias), the only config difference. `nxeon-vendor.yaml` is byte-identical on all five (md5 a7b21b71...).
- The scheduler already excludes nodes lacking a template (`nodesWithTemplate`), but only checks *presence by vmid*, not content or age.
- Proposal (R8): a per-node `TemplateRecord` table; build each template **once** on a build node and `zfs send | zstd | ssh zfs recv` the `@__base__` snapshot to the other nodes, then write the matching `qemu-server/<vmid>.conf` (a 1.75-4 GB transfer, a minute or two). Then the ZFS guid is identical everywhere and **drift detection is a one-line comparison of guids** (plus config hash and vendor-yaml md5) in a read-only sweep, run daily and shown in /admin. Pin the version on the server (`Server.templateVmid`) so reinstalls use the same source. Running servers are never affected by a template update: a full clone is independent, and a linked clone depends on the *specific old snapshot*, which is why a rebuild must get a new vmid and the old template stays until its last clone is gone (already documented in `golden-template.ts`).

### 4.5 Warm pool

Pre-provisioned VMs per popular plan and region, claimed at order time.

- **Stopped** pool entries (cloned, images preloaded): claim = set config + start, ~30-45 s to ready. After R1/R2 a cold provision is already ~60-120 s, so the gain is ~20-40 s.
- **Running** pool entries: claim in 5-10 s, but each idles pinned RAM (a 4 GB Minecraft shell x 2 per region = 8 GB, ~15% of one node, in regions that are already RAM-constrained) and needs per-claim re-keying (root password via guest agent, management key, SSH host keys, hostname, telemetry token, game env, correct memory/cores, IP/port already allocated in IPAM for the pool slot).
- Verdict: **not worth it before R1/R2**; revisit only for plain Ubuntu and Minecraft with real demand data. Capacity is the binding constraint, not clone time.

### 4.6 Parallelising independent steps (R6)

Safe candidates, each small:
- IP/ARP inventory (~4 s) and clone (5-8 s) run in parallel (IP is only needed for config).
- Allocate game and join-port forwards **before** `qm start` (ports are known from the family), sync NAT **once**, and drop the 2 later full 5-node syncs from the critical path (saves ~5 s and removes a fatal failure mode seen 4x on N5). Sync only the target node, not all five.
- Merge `ensureGuestAccess` + `verifyGuestIdentity` + `installManagementKey` + the first startup sample into one SSH session.
- SSH poll 5 s to 2 s; TCP game-port poll 10 s to 3 s.
- `runProvisionReadiness` (6-12 s tail) and the deployment email in parallel.
Total ~15-25 s. Low individual value; do after R1/R2.

### 4.7 Other items worth doing

- **iothread/ssd on `scsi0` in the template config** (new provisions inherit): `perf-hypervisor.md` P1-1. Free for new VMs.
- **`compression=lz4` on the `data` pools** of N1/N3/N4/N5 (off today; N2 on): new blocks only; also shrinks templates 1.4-1.7x as seen on N2 (9000 is 1.00 GB there vs 1.75 GB elsewhere). P1-2 in the hypervisor report.
- **Pin image digests** after a verified provision (`scripts/verify-game-provision.ts` already prints them).
- **Stale-template refresh**: weekly rebuild of the base templates from the current Ubuntu cloud image (the package step no longer needs to run at first boot, so security patches must come from a fresh template, not from first-boot apt).
